skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Approximate decimals to a given number of places
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Round a decimal to a stated number of decimal places or to the nearest whole number, tenth or hundredth.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Locate integers on a number line
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Locate and read positive and negative integers on a number line, including lines with scaled intervals.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Find the rule relating quantities in a table
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Determine the rule connecting the two rows of a table of values.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Plot and read points in all four quadrants
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Plot and record coordinates across all four quadrants of the number plane.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Convert between metric units of length
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Convert between millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres using the decimal place value system.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Investigate symmetry of quadrilaterals
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Identify line and rotational symmetry of quadrilaterals.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Use multipliers for percentage change
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Use multipliers such as $\times 1.05$ or $\times 0.87$ for percentage increase or decrease.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Convert between units for rates
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Convert rates such as km/h to m/s and vice versa.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Convert between decimal hours and hours–minutes–seconds
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Convert times between decimal form and sexagesimal form, e.g. $1.875$ h $= 1$ h $52$ min $30$ s, including with the calculator's DMS button.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Translate between words and algebraic expressions
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Generate algebraic expressions from descriptions and vice versa.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Substitute values into algebraic expressions
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Replace pronumerals with numbers and evaluate the result.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Substitute negative numbers into expressions
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Substitute negative values for pronumerals, writing each in brackets, then evaluate using the order of operations.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Solve 2-step linear equations
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Solve two-step linear equations by undoing operations in reverse order of BIDMAS, including grouping, e.g. $3x+8=14$ and $3(x+1)=15$.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Verify equation solutions by substitution
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Check a solution by substituting it back into the equation.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Solve equations from formulas
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Solve linear equations arising from substituting values into formulas.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Plot points on the Cartesian plane
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Plot and identify points, including non-integer coordinates, in all quadrants.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Generate an equation from a pattern
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Describe a number pattern in words and write its equation.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Move between representations of a linear relationship
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Connect pattern, equation, table, coordinates and graph of a linear relationship.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Apply an equation from a pattern
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Use a pattern's equation to find values for larger or smaller numbers.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Construct a table of values
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Substitute x-values, including negatives and fractional coefficients, into y = mx + c to complete a table of values.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Graph a linear relationship
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Graph a straight line from its equation and compare multiple lines.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Solve real-life linear relationship problems
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Describe and solve real-life problems modelled by linear relationships.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Recognise points that satisfy a line
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Verify that a point lies on a line by satisfying its equation, and find a missing coordinate of a point on the line.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Solve a linear equation graphically
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Use the graph of a line to solve a corresponding linear equation.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Find the intersection of two lines
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Graph two lines and identify and verify their point of intersection.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Find the equation y = mx + c from a table
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Find m (the change in y as x increases by 1) and c (the value of y when x = 0), write y = mx + c, and check it against every column.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Compare linear relationships from their equations
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Use y = mx + c to tell whether a line is increasing or decreasing (sign of the coefficient of x), which of two lines is steeper (size of the coefficient), whether two lines are parallel (equal coefficients), and whether they share a y-intercept (equal constant terms).

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Describe properties of special quadrilaterals
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Verify and describe side, angle and diagonal properties of special quadrilaterals.

skillReferenceCatalogue.title: Rearrange a linear equation to gradient-intercept form
skillReferenceCatalogue.blurb: Rearrange a linear equation such as $3x + 2y = -4$ into $y = mx + c$ and read off the gradient and $y$-intercept.

evidence.text:
**MA4-LIN-C-01** creates and displays number patterns and finds graphical solutions to problems involving linear relationships

**Plot and identify points on the Cartesian plane**

• Plot and label points on the Cartesian plane of given coordinates, including those with coordinates that are not whole numbers
• Identify and record the coordinates of given points on the Cartesian plane, including those with coordinates that are not whole numbers

**Plot linear relationships on the Cartesian plane**

• Construct a geometric pattern and record the results in a table of values
• Represent a given number pattern (including decreasing patterns) using a table of values
• Describe a number pattern in words and generate an equation using algebraic symbols
• Apply an equation generated from a pattern to calculate the corresponding value for a smaller or larger number
• Recognise that a linear relationship can be represented by a number pattern, an equation (or a rule using algebraic symbols), a table of values, a set of pairs of coordinates and a line graphed on a Cartesian plane, and move flexibly between these representations
• Explain that there are an infinite number of ordered pairs that satisfy a given linear relationship by extending a line joining a set of points on the Cartesian plane
• Compare similarities and differences of multiple straight-line graphs on the same set of axes using graphing applications
• Describe linear relationships in real-life contexts and solve related problems

**Solve linear equations using graphical techniques**

• Recognise that each point on the graph of a linear relationship satisfies the equation of a line
• Apply graphs of linear relationships to solve a corresponding linear equation using graphing applications
• Graph 2 intersecting lines on the same set of axes and identify the point of intersection using either graphing applications or a table of values
• Verify that the point of intersection satisfies the equations of both lines

The **origin (0,0)** is where the $x$-axis and $y$-axis meet.

Key Ideas
1. A Cartesian plane is a [[horizontal|28]] number line and a [[vertical|24]] number line.

3. We can label a position on a Cartesian plane using [[coordinates|31]].

5. A coordinate is written as $(x, y)$; it tells us the position of a point compared to the [[origin|20]].
6. The first number is called the $x$-coordinate. It tells us how much to move h[[orizontally|31]], the second number is called the [[y-coordinate|33]] it tells us how much to move [[vertically|28]].

sourceAtom.label: Sketch a Line from a Table of Values

evidence.text:
Sketch a Line from a Table of Values
Some equations are called **linear relationships** because when we plot their $(x,y)$ pairs, it forms a straight line.

1.  Construct a table of values by substituting $x$ values into the equation to find $y$.

2.  Plot the $(x,y)$ points on a Cartesian plane.

3.  Draw a straight line through the points and extend it.

evidence.text:
Finding the Rule from a Table of Values
If we have a table where the value of $x$ increases by 1, and the value of $y$ when $x = 0$,
then we can use this method to find the equation $y = mx + c$:

1. Find $\mathbf{m}$: This is how much $y$ changes by as $x$ increases by 1.
2. Find $\mathbf{c}$: This is the value of $y$ when $x = 0$.
3. Write the equation $y = mx + c$ and check it works for every column.

Check that your rule works for every column.

evidence.text:
Find the equation that describes this table of values. Select A, B, C, or D.

$x$	$-1$	$0$	$1$	$2$
$y$	$3$	$1$	$-1$	$-3$

**A   **   $y=2x+1$
**B**    $y=2x-1$
**C   **   $y=x-2$
**D**    $y=-2x+1$

evidence.text:
Apply the equation of a linear relationship to make predictions
If we want to make 25 pentagons, how many matches do we need?

Let $x = 25$
$y = 4x + 1$
$= 4(25) + 1$
$= 101$

We need 101 matches to make 25 pentagons.

If we have 73 matches, how many pentagons can we make?

Let $y = 73$
$73 = 4x + 1$
$72 = 4x$
$18 = x$

We can make 18 pentagons with 73 matches.
For $x = 25$: $y = 4(25) + 1 = 101$ matches.
For $y = 73$: $73 = 4x + 1 \implies 72 = 4x \implies x = 18$ pentagons.

sourceAtom.label: Variables
sourceAtom.description: Variables

evidence.text:
Variables
A **variable** is a quantity that can change.

**Examples**: Weight $w$, cost $c$, time $t$, distance $d$, speed $s$

The **dependent variable** depends on another variable.
It is the **second row** of a table of values.
It is the ****$y$** axis** of a graph.

The **independent variable** does not depend on anything.
It is the **first row** of a table of values.
It is the ****$x$** axis** of a graph.

Independent variable $x$	$0$	$1$	$2$	$3$
Dependent variable $y$	$3$	$5$	$7$	$9$

sourceAtom.label: Key Ideas
sourceAtom.description: Key Ideas

evidence.text:
Key Ideas
1. The independent variable is the first [[row|13]] of a table of values and always goes on the [[x|9]] axis.

2. The dependent variable is the second [[row|13]] of a table of values and always goes on the [[y|9]] axis.

3. For matchstick patterns:
a. The number of matches was the [[dependent|26]] variable.
b. The number of shapes was the [[independent|31]] variable.

4. For **age** and **height**:
a. [[height|20]] is the dependent variable, since it changes based on [[age|13]]
b. [[age|13]] is the independent variable, since it doesn’t depend on anything.

5. If you graph the dependent and independent variable, and you can draw a straight line through all the coordinates, then we say that the variables have a [[linear|20]] relationship.

findings.title: Repair lost table columns and stale answer alignment
findings.evidence: The original four-column tables have three data columns in the saved reconstruction. Answers in b and d still include y=1 and y=14 for removed first columns.
findings.rationale: An inconsistent task/answer pair confounds assessment of table-column to coordinate conversion.
findings.recommendation: Restore the omitted first column in each table and realign coordinate blanks and worked answers against the student source; retain all four part IDs.

findings.title: Change impossible-shortcut wording
findings.evidence: Both prompts ask why m or c cannot be found. The first table (x=7,2,11; y=25,15,33) has m=2; the other lacks a displayed zero column, not a determinable constant. Current answers qualify the shortcut but prompts do not.
findings.rationale: Students should recognise the limits of a method, not learn that information is mathematically insufficient when it is sufficient.
findings.recommendation: Ask why simple adjacent y differences cannot directly give m, and why c cannot be read directly. Explicitly promise later normalisation/back-extension methods.

findings.title: Qualify variable-role definitions
findings.evidence: The independent variable is described as not depending on anything and table positions as always fixed. The cloze repeats this.
findings.rationale: Input/output are roles within the chosen model; row placement is a presentation convention.
findings.recommendation: Use “chosen input in this model” and “output modelled as depending on that input”; present the usual axis convention and a transposed-table contrast.

findings.title: Distinguish nonvertical form, zero slope and coincident lines
findings.evidence: Page 23 generalises y=mx+c; page 73 says equal coefficients imply parallel lines. Page 92 includes x=3 and page 93 correctly says two different lines.
findings.rationale: The missing qualifiers affect both classification and simultaneous-solution reasoning.
findings.recommendation: State nonvertical scope, include m=0, and compare y=2x+1 with y=2x−3 and 2y=4x+2. Distinguish distinct parallel lines from the same line. Preserve the already-correct nonvertical qualifier on page 77.

findings.title: Teach table-column recognition before using it
findings.evidence: Q2 requires plotting table coordinates before the Identify concept and Q3 explain column→pair conversion.
findings.rationale: This is an identifiable intermediate atom between substitution and plotting.
findings.recommendation: Use Q1 review → Identify concept → Q3 pair conversion → Q2 table plotting → Q4 chain; keep each question with its own table and diagram.

position.current: page 15: Q1, Q2, Identify, Q3, Q4
position.recommended: page 15: Q1, Identify, Q3, Q2, Q4

findings.title: Prepare two-operation and inverse table branches
findings.evidence: The two-operation rule example asserts the combined rule before m/c isolation on 29–30. Page 27 Q4 has unknown input entries; the forward/inverse review occurs on 50.
findings.rationale: Familiar single-operation rules do not establish every recognition and inverse-solving decision.
findings.recommendation: Keep one-operation example/practice first; place the two-operation example and dependent guided part after the m/c base chain (or provide that isolation locally). Add a two-item substitute-and-solve review before Q4 without moving its shared tables.

position.current: two-operation example/guided on 25; inverse table on 27; preparation on 29–30 and 50
position.recommended: single-operation 25–26 → base m/c preparation → two-operation example/guided; inverse review immediately before 27 Q4

findings.title: Match early worked answers to the method taught
findings.evidence: Several saved worked answers use intercept language, difference quotients or c=y−mx before the relevant branch has been introduced. Early table tasks can be solved by unit differences and reading/extension to zero.
findings.rationale: A valid advanced solution can hide the intended teachable chain and falsely imply new student prerequisites.
findings.recommendation: Show the taught table/substitution route first; label later-method alternatives explicitly. Do not add Stage 5 gradient-formula mappings merely because an answer uses that notation.

findings.title: Make harder table branches and selection explicit
findings.evidence: Back-extension has a first completed scaffold; non-unit steps explicitly say to divide and begin with 8÷2. Parameter substitution then introduces another decision, including avoiding x=0 when finding m.
findings.rationale: There is partial preparation, not a wholesale absence of teaching. Students need to know when each method applies.
findings.recommendation: Add a short We Do after each first scaffold, a substitution/equation review before 37, then retain 38 as mixed method selection. Ask students to name the method before computing on a few contrasts.

position.current: branches embedded in Development/Mastery practice on 33–37
position.recommended: explicit small chunks at 33,35,37, each with example→guided→independent; mixed selection stays on 38

findings.title: Add a scale-reading bridge and resolve scale provenance
findings.evidence: Fractional coordinates appear in early plotting; page 41 explicitly warns that axis scales differ. Source Q5 a–c use y intervals of 2; saved diagram model step metadata differs in a–c.
findings.rationale: Counting squares as units is an at-risk recognition error. Model metadata alone does not prove a rendered student diagram is wrong.
findings.recommendation: Teach unit-per-interval before fractional/unequal-scale work. For page 41 compare the current rendered diagrams, model and source before repair; treat the rendering discrepancy as unresolved, and retain the source scale as evidence.

findings.title: Respect graph windows and supplied graph scaffolds
findings.evidence: The page 16 example tabulates (3,7) beyond a grid ending at y=5. Page 44 guided graph panels already contain lines in both source and saved diagrams. A pending Studio operation would remove labelled points from page 39 Q2a.
findings.rationale: Window selection is a decision; a supplied graph does not independently assess construction. Labelled coordinates can be intentional fading support.
findings.recommendation: Explain plotting visible points and extending the line, or choose a suitable scale. Treat supplied graphs on 44 as read/check guided facets, with blank independent graphs on 45. Leave the pending page 39 operation undecided; evaluate its scaffold purpose before later acceptance.

findings.title: Add the short graph-to-table-to-rule example
findings.evidence: Page 39 begins with Foundation tasks, scaffolded tables and labelled coordinates, but no complete worked chain.
findings.rationale: Reading points and finding a table rule are familiar; the selection and ordering of points connects them.
findings.recommendation: Show one general example such as y=2x+1: read two/three convenient points in ascending x → table → rule → check another point. Follow with changed numbers and fade table labels. Keep the Stage 4 table method.

findings.title: Prepare count feasibility and requested-quantity decisions
findings.evidence: Q12 asks whether 543 sticks fits y=3x+2, yielding a noninteger x. Q13 changes between shaded/unshaded/total. Page 61 Q6 decreases 6,5,4,3 triangles, but asks for x=17; y=7−x then gives −10. Its saved alternative text describes the fourth picture as two triangles.
findings.rationale: Feasibility and quantity choice are additional atoms. A formal extrapolation is not a physical negative count.
findings.recommendation: Add possible/impossible count and shaded/total contrasts before the challenge. Label page 61 Q6 as formal extrapolation versus physical domain, and repair its alt text from the four source pictures; preserve the equation’s arithmetic.

findings.title: Isolate modelling decisions and conditional unit prerequisites
findings.evidence: The taxi investigation combines variables, rate/fixed fee, equation, table, graph and prediction. Later items require mixed time units, percentage multipliers and rate conversion.
findings.rationale: The common linear chain is familiar; fixed/rate selection and context-specific conversions are not interchangeable with graphing.
findings.recommendation: Before 66, distinguish a starting fee from cost per unit in one worked/guided pair. Add concise prerequisite cues before the affected conversion/percentage items; map those parts to their existing skills, not every linear-real-life target. Retain page 70’s impossible-height/limitation pair.

findings.title: Bring line selection ahead of full graphical solving
findings.evidence: Pages 82–83 ask for graphical solves before page 84 isolates the choice y=mx+c and y=k.
findings.rationale: Method selection should be available before the full routine; membership investigation remains useful beforehand.
findings.recommendation: Keep 81 review and 82 membership discussion. Insert the complete 84 line-selection group before the solving portion of 82/83, with a horizontal-versus-vertical contrast. Keep shared page 82 graph/stem with any separated subquestions.

position.current: 81 review → 82/83 full investigations → 84 line selection → 85 worked/guided
position.recommended: 81 review → 82 membership → 84 line selection → 85 worked/guided → 82/83 solve/context applications

findings.title: Teach verification of both equations and separate extension demands
findings.evidence: Page 92 requires substituting an intersection into both equations. Page 93 e–h requires rearrangement of implicit equations; Q6 adds parameters.
findings.rationale: Verification is a characteristic part of the Stage 4 public skill. Implicit rearrangement is a later-stage conditional demand.
findings.recommendation: After intersection reading, model checking one pair in both equations, then keep 92 Q2 as guided-to-independent practice. Place 93 Q5e–h and Q6 in an explicit extension group with rearrangement preparation; preserve their shared stems.

findings.title: Create a cumulative independent endpoint and usable teaching chunks
findings.evidence: There is mixed practice within table-method, representation and comparison sections, but the final pages are concentrated on simultaneous equations and extension rather than a cumulative independent mix of all booklet routines. Saved sections are source pages.
findings.rationale: Local mixed practice does not supply the booklet contract’s final interleaved coverage. Page boundaries are not teaching module boundaries.
findings.recommendation: Use the 13 instructional chunks in this audit as a proposed grouping layer. Add a final independent set mixing coordinates, tables, rule selection, forward/inverse modelling, comparison, graphical solve and verification, plus one synthesis challenge. Use fresh surfaces, retain existing dependent groups, and keep optional extension separate.

position.current: 93 source-page sections; final endpoint is simultaneous equations
position.recommended: 13 teaching chunks with mini mixed checks, followed by a cumulative independent mix and challenge

findings.title: Replace blanket block mappings with demand-specific roles and links
findings.evidence: All 233 saved mappings are block-level proposals. Examples include number-line review labelled Cartesian plotting, all page 42 review labelled pattern work, and compound leaves whose table/rule/graph facets cannot share one mastery claim.
findings.rationale: A page topic is not evidence that every target teaches or assesses its full public skill.
findings.recommendation: Use register recommendations at part/facet grain; retain direct versus inherited mapping provenance. Treat review as prerequisite practice, worked examples as teaching, guided response as practice and suitable unscaffolded items as assessment opportunities. Do not infer student mastery from this audit.

findings.title: Tighten contrasts, recall and response criteria
findings.evidence: The first nonlinear/linear contrast on 23 changes both exponent and coefficient. Signed-input plus signed-coefficient combination appears in guided substitution. Point membership is explicit on 82, but infinitely many real solution pairs are not checked directly. Page 93 requests an estimate.
findings.rationale: Small recognition contrasts and explicit response criteria expose hidden decisions without proliferating public skills.
findings.recommendation: Use a minimal-change nonlinear/linear pair, e.g. 2x²+3 versus 2x+3; check a double-negative substitution; retain existing comparison contrasts; ask why points between two plotted points are also solutions; specify an acceptable estimate interval based on the grid.

fourPartTest.distinctive: Verification of the same ordered pair in each line equation is part of the target blurb, and point-satisfies-line is its simplest specialist enabler.
fourPartTest.atRisk: A visually plausible crossing may be misread; checking only one equation does not establish simultaneous satisfaction.
fourPartTest.stageCourse: Both Stage 4; prerequisite explicitly available in s4, the target’s course.
fourPartTest.nonRedundant: No path from intersection-of-lines to point-satisfies-line in baseline graph; shared ancestors are not reachability.

blurbChanges.before: Use y = mx + c to tell whether a line is increasing or decreasing (sign of the coefficient of x), which of two lines is steeper (size of the coefficient), whether two lines are parallel (equal coefficients), and whether they share a y-intercept (equal constant terms).
blurbChanges.after: For nonvertical lines written as y = mx + c, use the sign of m to identify increasing, decreasing or horizontal lines, compare |m| for steepness on equally scaled axes, and use equal c values to identify a shared y-intercept. Equal m with different c gives distinct parallel lines; equal m and c gives the same line.
blurbChanges.rationale: Clarifies boundaries already inherent in comparison; no new skill, stage, course or dot-point scope.
